doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: The early-eighties slump
summary: Dorn compares producers to running backs and recalls the early eighties when the business changed and he could not get work. He then ran his own companies.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: You had a few years, your son described —
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Bottom fell out.

Listen, record producers are really like running backs in the NFL. You get your three, four, five years you know? This is 46 years coming up on that I’m doing this. I had a very ugly period in the early eighties, I couldn’t get any work. The music was changing and I was still doing what I did you know. And also the structure of the business was changing, so they didn’t need any wildcat producers anymore, you know there were A&R staffs and there were rules, and I just imagined somebody telling a painter hey, paintings that are selling now don’t have trees. Steer clear of trees. Don’t paint trees. Just oceans. We’re selling oceans. You know. And it turned into that. And I wasn’t good at that. I’m not good at that now. You know like I always have my own companies, I do what I want to do, you know. I do what I want to do because I like to do what I like to do, and also, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

don’t know how to do anything other than what I do. So if there’s no company to do it at I’ve got to have my own company. So pretty much everything I’ve done for the last 25 years, once I got out of that early eighties slump, is follow my instincts like I did when I got hired at Atlantic. Nesuhi said go get ‘em. So I got Rahsaan and I got Yusef and I got Les and you know Eddie and all those things and that stuff really worked.
